The bay at Ostler’s Reach lost its eelgrass in the winter of 1932, when a wasting disease moved through the shallows, and for sixty years the bottom was bare sand. Eelgrass is not seaweed. It is a flowering plant that went back into the sea, with roots, and pollen, and seeds the size of a grain of rice, and where it grows it holds the sediment down and gives young fish somewhere to be.

In 1994 a county biologist named Ruth Feather began putting it back. The method was simple and unglamorous: divers collected flowering shoots from a healthy meadow at Calder Point, ten miles east, kept them in tanks until the seeds dropped, and then sowed the seeds by hand into the bare bottom at Ostler’s Reach in the autumn. The first plots came up thick. Photographs from the following July show a green field where the sand had been, and the county printed one of them on the cover of its annual report.

Four winters later most of it was gone. Not eaten, not dug up — simply thinned, patch by patch, until the plots were as bare as the bottom around them. Feather had recorded everything about the water and almost nothing about the plants, so the first search went where the records were. The temperature record showed nothing unusual. The salinity record showed nothing unusual. A colleague suggested, without much conviction, that the trouble might be in the seed rather than in the site.

Feather had sown from Calder Point because it was the nearest healthy meadow and because a boat could reach it in an hour. That meadow, it turned out, was itself the survivor of the 1932 die-off: a few clumps that had lived through it and had spread, over sixty years, by sending out runners. Eelgrass that spreads by runners makes copies of itself. Nearly every shoot the divers had collected was, genetically, the same plant, and whatever killed one of them in a bad August killed the rest on the same afternoon.

The second attempt, begun in 2001, collected from eleven meadows spread along ninety miles of coast, including three that were thin and unimpressive and would never have been chosen on the strength of their appearance. Those plots have now survived two hot summers and a hurricane. Feather is careful about what this proves. Mixed plots have done better here, in one bay, for twenty years; the mechanism is plausible and the sample is one. What she will say without qualification is that the first attempt was not a failure of effort, and that the county’s cover photograph was taken during the part of the experiment that always looks good.

Between 1867 and 1961 a private company in Hartsville drew and redrew maps of American towns for the use of fire insurers. An underwriter in a distant city could not visit Mineral Springs, Ohio, before writing a policy on a hardware store there, so the company sold him a page on which the store was drawn to scale, with its depth in feet, the number of its storeys, the position of its windows, and — in colour — what it was built of. Stone and brick were blue. Wood was yellow. A yellow block with no water main near it cost more to insure than a blue one.

The colours were chosen for money, not for history. The company had no interest in what a town had been; it wanted to know what would burn. Yet because the surveyors returned to the same towns every few years and redrew what they found, the sheets record something the decennial census never asked about: which buildings a town replaced, and with what.

Consider a block in Mineral Springs that appears on four sheets. In 1885 it is a row of yellow rectangles, a livery stable among them. In 1892 the middle four are blue and half again as deep. In 1904 the whole row is blue, and the stable is labelled as a garage. In 1916 the block is blue and unchanged. The census for those years counts the people of Mineral Springs and reports their occupations; it says nothing whatever about the row. A historian who wants to know when the town stopped building in timber cannot ask the census. She can count rectangles.

This has made the sheets popular with people the company never imagined serving, and the popularity has brought its own difficulty. The surveyors were paid by the sheet, and a surveyor behind on his route had reasons to copy the last edition rather than walk the block again. Where a building is drawn identically across three editions, the historian cannot tell a town that did not change from a surveyor who did not look. Some of the sheets can be checked against fire-department records, deeds and photographs; most cannot.

The maps are therefore neither the archive they are sometimes called nor the mere commercial leavings they were. They are a long, uneven series of observations made for one purpose and readable for another, and the second use is only ever as good as the first work was careful.

An underwriter in a distant city could not visit Mineral Springs, Ohio, before writing a policy on a hardware store there, so the company sold him a page on which the store was drawn to scale, with its depth in feet, the number of its storeys, the position of its windows, and — in colour — what it was built of. Stone and brick were blue. Wood was yellow. A yellow block with no water main near it cost more to insure than a blue one.

The Kalvala of the Setu — no relation to the Finnish poem of the similar name — is a cycle of about four thousand lines sung in a border district between two countries, and it was first put into English by Margery Aldiss in 1959. Aldiss had lived in the district for six years and her version has never quite gone out of print. It also has nine hundred footnotes.

The notes are not scholarly ornament. The cycle’s singers assume a listener who knows the district: who knows that the “black field” is a particular field, that a man who arrives “from the water side” arrives from the direction of a village the audience could name, and that the small joke in the fourteenth song turns on two words that sound alike in the local speech and in no other. Aldiss held that a reader who did not know these things was not reading the poem, and she supplied them at the foot of the page — sometimes four notes to a line.

In 1981 she published a second version. It has the same translator, the same source and eleven footnotes. She had not changed her mind about what the reader needed to know. She had changed her mind about where it should go. The 1981 text puts a plain word where a local one had stood — “the burial field” for “the black field” — and, where a joke cannot survive, it says in the line itself that the singers laugh here. Everything else went into a fifty-page essay at the front, to be read once, before the poem.

Reviewers were divided, and the division was not about accuracy. Those who preferred 1959 said that a translation which smooths the strangeness away teaches the reader that the poem is like a poem in English, which is the one thing it is not. Those who preferred 1981 said that a reader who stops at every line to look down at the foot of the page never hears the cycle as a cycle, and that a poem sung through in a single evening cannot be met in fragments.

Aldiss herself, asked about it in 1984, said that the two books were made for two different readers and that she did not regret either. Her only complaint about the argument, she said, was that both sides talked as though a reader’s attention were unlimited, when it is the scarcest thing a poem has to spend.

A city loses water between the reservoir and the tap, and nobody can see where. The pipe is underground; the leak is a hole the size of a coin; the ground swallows the evidence. For most of the twentieth century the trade’s answer was to listen. A leak in a pressurised main makes a steady hiss, and the sound travels along the metal of the pipe for a surprising distance, so a man with a listening stick pressed to a hydrant could hear a hole a hundred metres away. The work was done between midnight and four, because traffic, washing machines and pumps all make noise in the same range.

Ramona Suess ran the leak crew in Brant for nine years, and the maps she inherited showed the loss concentrated in the old districts on the hill, where the pipes were cast iron laid in the 1890s. That is where the crews went, and that is where they found leaks, and the arithmetic of the annual report followed the crews.

In her third year the city put pressure loggers into every district, for a different reason: a rule made by the state required them. A logger records the pressure in a district minute by minute, and a district with a leak loses pressure at night, when nothing else is drawing. The loggers reported the loss from the hill districts at about the figure the crews had always given. They also reported, in two districts of post-war plastic pipe at the bottom of the town, a night loss half again as large as anything on the hill, which no crew had ever recorded and no resident had ever complained about.

Plastic does not carry sound the way cast iron does. A hiss in a plastic main dies out within a few metres of the hole, so a listening stick at a hydrant hears an empty pipe. The crews had not been missing the plastic districts through carelessness. They had been searching with an instrument that cannot detect the thing they were looking for, in the one place where it mattered, and the maps that told them where to go had been drawn from their own results.

Brant now runs both. The loggers say which district; the sticks, where the pipes are iron, say which street. Suess is blunt about the years before: the crews were skilled and the reports were honest, and the number at the bottom of each report was a description of where the crews had been.
